To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the closure of the local fishery for sea cucumber in 2009 resulted in an average decline in annual shark fin production of 75%, from 1,500 kg to 375 kg.

(1) the recent closure of Papua New Guinea's sea cucumber fishery has had a major impact on local shark fin production and (2) community-based management options for the small-scale shark fishery should be considered.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the trade-off between community welfare and conservation and shows that the closure of the local, but globally important, sea cucumber fishery has had an adverse effect on the welfare of Louisiade fishers, and that the management of shark resources is likely to be a more effective way of improving fishers' welfare than the management of shark fin production.

the trade-off between conservation and community well-being.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Louisiade shark fin fishery is currently underutilised.
there are no clear-cut management options for artisanal shark fishing in Papua New Guinea, as the socio-economic context is so complex.
the local shark fin fishery is not currently a major source of income for local communities in the Louisiades.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the local fishery is in decline and is likely to continue declining unless the local economy is diversified and/or the sea cucumber fisher is reopened.
the local communities in the study area have been negatively impacted by a combination of market and policy factors.

the local communities of the Louisiade archipelago have a high dependence on marine resources and are likely to be highly vulnerable to the loss of these resources, especially if there is a lack of alternative income opportunities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the socio-economic context of a fishery should be carefully considered in the development of management options.
the management of shark resources in this region should be based on the socio-economic characteristics of the local communities and their fishing practices.

the trade-off between conservation and community wellbeing in the case of shark fisheries is likely to be less severe in the case of the small-scale fisheries in Papua New Guinean waters than has been previously thought.
